source_text: aliam illi regulam praetendo: sicut naturalia, ita rationalia esse debere in deo omnia. exigo rationem bonitatis, quia nec aliud quid bonum haberi liceat, quod non rationaliter bonum sit, nedum ut ipsa bonitas inrationalis deprehendatur. facilius malum, cui rationis aliquid adfuerit, pro bono habebitur quam ut bonum ratone desertum non pro malo iudicetur. nego rationalem bonitatem\', dei Marcionis iam hoc primo, quod in salutem processerit; hominis alieni. scio dicturos atquin hanc esse principalem \' et perfectam bonitatem, cum sine ullo debito familiaritatis iri extraneos uoluntaria et libera effundatur, secundum quam inimicos quoque nostros et hoc nomine iam extraneos diligere iubeamur. cur ergo non a primordio hominem respexit. a primordio extraneum? cessando praeiudicauit cum extraneo nihil sibi esse. ceterum disciplinam diligendi extraneum uel inimicum antecessit praeceptum diligendi proximum tamquam te ipsum. quod etsi ex lege creatoris, et tu quoque illud excipere debebis, ut a Christo non destructum, sed potius exstructum. nam quo magis proximum diligas, diligere iuberis inimicum et extraneum. exaggeratio est debitae bonitatis exactio indebitae. antecedit autem debita indebitam, ut principalis, ut dignior, ut ministra et comite sua [id est indebita] prior. igitur cum prima bonitatis ratio sit in rem suam exhiberi ex iustitia, secunda autem in alienam ex redundantia iustitiae super scribarum et Pharisaeorum, quale est secundam ei rationem referri, cui deficit prima, non habenti proprium hominem ac per hoc quoque exiguae? porro exigua, quae suum non habuit, quomodo in alienum redundauit? exhibe principalem rationem, et tunc uindica sequentem. nulla res sine ordine rationalis potest uindicari; tanto abest, ut ratio ipsa in aliquo ordinem amittat. sit nunc et a secundo gradu incipiens ratio bonitatis, in extraneum scilicet: nec secundus illi gradus ratione constabit, alio modo destructus. tunc enim rationalis habebitur uel secunda in extraneum bonitas, si sine iniuria eius operetur, cuius est res. quamcumque bonitatem iustitia prima efficit rationalem. sicut in principali gradu, cum in rem suam exhibetur, rationalis erit si iusta sit, sic et in extraneum rationalis uideri poterit, si non sit iniusta. ceterum qualis bonitas quae per iniuriam constat, et quidem pro extraneo? fortasse enim pro domestico aliquatenus rationalis habeatur bonitas iniuriosa. pro extraneo uero, cui nec proba legitime deberetur, qua ratione tam iniusta rationalis defendetur? quid enim iniustius, quid iniquius et improbius quam ita alieno benefacere seruo, ut domino eripiatur, ut alii uindicetur, ut aduersus caput domini subornetur, et quidem, quod indignius, in ipsa adhuc domo domini, de ipsius adhuc horreis uiuens, sub ipsius adhuc plagis tremens? talis adsertor etiam damnaretur in saeculo, nedum plagiator. non aliter ** deus Marcionis, inrumpens in alienum mundum, eripiens deo hominem, patri filium, educatori aluminum, domino famulum, ut eum efficiat deo impium, patri inreligiosum, educatori ingratum, domino nequam. oro te, si rationalis bonitas talem facit, qualem faceret inrationalis? non putem impudentiorem quam qui in aliena aqua alii deo tingitur, ad alienum caelum alii deo expanditur, in aliena terra alii deo sternitur, super alienum panem alii deo gratiarum actionibus fungitur, de alienis bonis ob alium deum nomine elemosynae et dilectionis operatur. quis iste deus tam bonus, ut homo ab illo malus fiat, tam propitius, ut alium illi deum, et dominum quidem ipsius, faciat iratum?
pass_a_gloss: I propose to him another rule: just as natural things, so also rational things ought to be in God. I demand a reason for goodness, because no other thing can be considered good unless it is rationally good, and certainly not that goodness itself is irrational. It is easier for evil, to which some reason has been added, to be considered good than for good, deserted by reason, not to be judged as evil. I deny rational goodness to Marcion's God, first because he proceeded to the salvation of a foreign man; I know they will say that this is the principal and perfect goodness, because it is voluntarily and freely poured out on foreigners without any debt of familiarity, according to which we are also commanded to love our enemies, who are also foreigners by this name. Why, then, did he not regard man from the beginning as a foreigner from the beginning? By ceasing, he prejudged that he had nothing to do with the foreigner. Moreover, the discipline of loving a foreigner or enemy preceded the command to love one's neighbor as oneself. Although this is from the law of the Creator, you also ought to accept it, as not destroyed by Christ, but rather built upon. For the more you love your neighbor, the more you are commanded to love your enemy and foreigner. The exacting of debtless goodness is an exaggeration of owed goodness. But owed goodness precedes debtless goodness, as principal, as more worthy, as minister and companion to its own, that is, debtless goodness. Therefore, when the first reason for goodness is to exhibit it to one's own out of justice, and the second is to exhibit it to a foreigner out of the abundance of justice, what kind of second reason can be referred to him who lacks the first, and does not have his own man, and therefore is also deficient? Furthermore, what is deficient, which did not have its own, how did it abound to a foreigner? Show the principal reason, and then vindicate the subsequent one. No thing can be vindicated without order; so much so that reason itself does not lose order in anything. Let the reason for goodness now begin from the second degree, namely, in the foreigner: nor will the second degree of goodness be consistent with reason, having been destroyed in another way. Then, indeed, goodness towards a foreigner will be considered rational if it operates without injury to him whose thing it is. Whatever goodness justice first effects is rational. Just as in the principal degree, when it is exhibited to one's own, it will be rational if it is just, so also in the foreigner it can be seen as rational if it is not unjust. But what kind of goodness is it that consists through injury, and indeed for a foreigner? Perhaps, indeed, goodness that is injurious can be considered rational for a domestic servant to some extent. But for a foreigner, to whom not even legitimate goodness is owed, by what reason can such unjust goodness be defended as rational? What, indeed, is more unjust, more iniquitous, and more wicked than to benefit a foreign servant in such a way that it is taken away from the master, vindicated to another, and suborned against the head of the master, and, indeed, what is more unworthy, while still living in the master's house, from the master's stores, trembling under the master's blows? Such a defender would also be condemned in the world, not to mention the plagiarist. Not otherwise does Marcion's God, bursting into a foreign world, taking man away from God, son away from father, pupil away from teacher, servant away from master, so that he makes him impious to God, irreligious to father, ungrateful to teacher, and wicked to master. I ask you, if rational goodness makes such a person, what would irrational goodness do? I do not think anyone is more shameless than one who is baptized in another's water to another god, expands to another god's heaven, is laid out on another god's earth, performs thanksgiving actions to another god over another's bread, and operates with another's goods in the name of elemosynary and love for another god. What kind of god is this, so good that man becomes evil from him, so propitious that he makes another god, and indeed the master of him, angry?

pass_b_english: I lay down another rule for him: just as the natural order is rational, so everything in God must be rational. I demand a rational basis for goodness, because nothing can be considered good unless it is rationally good, let alone that goodness itself should be found irrational. It is easier for evil, once some reason is attached to it, to pass for good than for good, abandoned by reason, to escape being judged evil. I deny rational goodness to Marcion's God, first of all because he proceeded to the salvation of a foreign man. I know they will retort that this is the principal and perfect goodness, since it is voluntarily and freely poured out on strangers without any debt of kinship, in accordance with which we are commanded to love even our enemies, who are strangers by that very name. Why, then, did he not regard man from the beginning as a stranger from the beginning? By holding back, he prejudged that he had nothing to do with the stranger. Besides, the discipline of loving a stranger or enemy came before the command to love one's neighbor as oneself. Even though this comes from the Creator's Law, you too must accept it, as not destroyed by Christ but rather built upon. For the more you love your neighbor, the more you are commanded to love your enemy and the stranger. Exacting debtless goodness is an exaggeration of owed goodness. But owed goodness precedes debtless goodness, as the principal, as the worthier, as the minister and companion of its own, that is, debtless goodness. Therefore, when the first rationale for goodness is to show it to one's own out of justice, and the second is to show it to a stranger out of the overflow of justice beyond the scribes and Pharisees, what kind of second rationale can be assigned to one who lacks the first, who does not possess his own man, and is therefore deficient even in that smaller measure? Moreover, how did what is deficient, which did not have its own, abound to a stranger? Produce the primary rationale, and then vindicate the subsequent one. Nothing can be vindicated without rational order; so far is it from reason itself losing order in anything. Let the rationale for goodness now begin from the second degree, namely toward the stranger: nor will that second degree stand with reason, since it has been destroyed in another way. For then, indeed, goodness toward a stranger would be considered rational if it operates without injury to him whose property it is. Whatever goodness justice first effects is rational. Just as in the primary degree, when it is shown to one's own, it will be rational if it is just, so also toward a stranger it can be seen as rational if it is not unjust. But what kind of goodness consists through injury, and that for a stranger? Perhaps, indeed, injurious goodness might be considered rational to some extent for a household servant. But for a stranger, to whom not even legitimate goodness is owed, by what reason can such unjust goodness be defended as rational? What is more unjust, more iniquitous, and more wicked than to benefit a stranger's servant in such a way that he is snatched from his master, vindicated to another, and suborned against his master's head — and, what is more unworthy, while still living in his master's house, from his master's stores, trembling under his master's blows? Such a defender would be condemned even in the world, let alone the plagiarist. In no other way does Marcion's God, bursting into a foreign world, tear man away from God, son from father, pupil from teacher, servant from master, so that he makes him impious toward God, irreligious toward his father, ungrateful toward his teacher, and wicked toward his master. I ask you: if rational goodness produces such a man, what would irrational goodness produce? I do not think anyone more shameless than the one who is baptized in another's water to another god, expands to another god's heaven, is laid out on another god's earth, offers thanksgiving over another's bread to another god, and operates with another's goods in the name of almsgiving and love for another god. What kind of god is this, so good that man becomes evil from him, so gracious that he makes another god — and indeed his own master — angry?
